Where it began

Jonny Bairstow was born in Bradford on 26 September 1989 into a cricketing family. His father, David Bairstow, kept wicket for Yorkshire and England and taught Jonny how to play, and his elder half-brother Andrew played for Derbyshire.

At St Peter's School in York he played fly-half at rugby and right-back at football, and he spent eight years in the Leeds United Academy, but cricket won in the end. In 2008 he became the first winner of Wisden's Young Schools Cricketer of the Year, having made 654 runs for St Peter's the summer before.

The player

He first played for Yorkshire in 2009, and in 2015 he piled up 1,108 Championship runs at 92.33 as they won the title again.

Geoffrey Boycott, a close friend of the family, presented him with his England cap at Lord's in May 2012. He went on to play 100 Tests up to 2024, scoring 6,042 runs at 36.40 with 12 hundreds, 26 fifties and a best of 167 not out. As keeper he held 205 catches and made 14 stumpings. When he kept wicket in the last two Tests of the 2013–14 Ashes, he and David became the first father and son both to keep for England in Tests. He was also part of the side that won the 2019 World Cup.

What made him special

He loved a crisis, and with England four or five down he would go on the attack. At Newlands in 2015–16 he and Ben Stokes put on 399 for the sixth wicket, a world record, and Bairstow had his first Test hundred, 150 not out. In 2022 he made six Test hundreds in the calendar year, one of them reached in 77 balls to chase down New Zealand at Trent Bridge. Against India that summer he made a century in each innings, the second in an unbroken stand of 269 with Joe Root as England chased 378, their highest successful chase in Tests. Those two hundreds earned him the first Wisden Trophy.

His batting coach Mark Ramprakash saw him as instinctive rather than tidy, and at his best on the attack. For a while England were never quite sure whether to pick him as a batter or a keeper. In the end they mostly picked him as both.

Away from the middle

The honours came in a rush after 2022: the PCA Men's Cricketer of the Year award, the Cricket Writers' Club Bob Willis Trophy and a place in the ICC Test Team of the Year. In 2017 he wrote an autobiography, A Clear Blue Sky, with Duncan Hamilton, and in March 2025 Yorkshire made him their red-ball captain.

And finally

At Old Trafford in the 2023 Ashes he was left on 99 not out when England's last wicket fell, only the third time that had happened in an Ashes Test. The other two were Boycott and Steve Waugh, which is decent company. Five years earlier, in a T10 match in Sharjah, he had shown what happens when there is no time to get stuck: 84 not out from 24 balls, a record for the format.
